According to the Defender of Rights 2020 report, biased data can contribute to algorithmic discrimination by reflecting past discriminatory practices and systemic discrimination present in society. For instance, if an algorithm is trained on employment data where women are underrepresented and occupy lower positions, it may deduce that women are less productive than men, thereby reproducing and exacerbating existing biases in recruitment processes.

On the other hand, apparently neutral criteria can also lead to discriminatory effects. The report highlights that using seemingly neutral criteria, such as the institution of origin in university algorithms, can indirectly discriminate against certain groups, like youths of foreign origin, due to existing residential and educational segregation. This means that even criteria that do not explicitly include prohibited grounds for discrimination can still result in biased outcomes when they correlate with protected characteristics. Thus, both biased data and neutral criteria can work together to create and perpetuate algorithmic discrimination.
